proposed_edges.relationship: DuVal: in the Arkansas Valley Native peoples dominated and incorporated colonists; 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006)
proposed_edges.map_label: DuVal: native ground, not middle ground, 2006
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Kathleen DuVal's argument (The Native Ground, 2006), not a verdict of the field. Introduction unread; the central sentence, p. 5, is witnessed identically by two readers read here: Piker (AHR 112:3, 2007, extract read) and Isaac (ActiveHistory, 2021, read in full). Piker also quotes p. 5: colonialism 'met neither accommodation nor resistance but incorporation'. Hatfield (Common-Place 7:2, 2007, read in full): DuVal 'argues that unlike the peoples of the Great Lakes region Richard White studies … Arkansas Indians dominated their region well into the nineteenth century … because they were not a population of refugees as were the Indians in the Great Lakes'. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.4)

proposed_edges.relationship: Hämäläinen: Comanche power left 'little or no middle ground for compromise between Indians and non-Indians' (Grillot on The Comanche Empire, 2008); White's 2011 preface agrees that in this case 'no middle ground emerges'
proposed_edges.map_label: Hämäläinen: Comanche empire, no middle ground, 2008
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Pekka Hämäläinen's book as read by Thomas Grillot (Books & Ideas, 20 January 2014, read in full): 'There is little or no middle ground for compromise between Indians and non-Indians in his book (p. 130): the Comanches are too powerful for this'; Grillot also judges that 'the criticism of the concept of the middle ground … seems here to have been pushed too far'. The book itself is unread. White's own reading of it, 2011 preface p. xv (Google Books snippet, source pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_preface_2011): 'no middle ground emerges'. Grillot records that White signed the preface to the French translation. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.5)

proposed_edges.relationship: Witgen: in a Native New World the French moved, as Reda puts it, from misunderstanding to being 'essentially delusional' about their relations; European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Michael Witgen's book as read by John Reda (H-AmIndian, July 2014, read in full), p. 2: 'Up to this point, Witgen's explanation seems little different from Richard White's middle ground, where cultural misinterpretations often led to workable understandings between Europeans and Native Americans. Witgen, however, pushes further to demonstrate that the French passed quickly from misunderstanding Native Americans to becoming essentially delusional about the nature of their relationships with them.' Witgen as quoted by Reda: 'the possession of large portions of Native North America by the empires of Europe never occurred' (p. 28); the British 'simply inherited the illusion of empire' (p. 217). 'Delusional' is Reda's word, not Witgen's. The book is unread. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.6)

proposed_edges.relationship: White in 2021 (interview published in Portuguese translation): the more anthropology he read, the more critical he became of ethnohistory as a hybrid, and he is increasingly wary of upstreaming; the New Indian History now looks primitive, and its agency argument could go too far
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrase only. Fontella, História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054 (read in full): White's English answers, received 30 April 2021, are published only in Fontella's Portuguese translation, so no English words are attributed to him. p. 10: 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; 'A New Indian History parece bastante primitiva agora … a tendência poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 15: 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16: upstreaming assumes that a belief, ritual or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda significativamente à medida que viaja no tempo'. The later worry about agency is his own; it is not evidence about Brownlie and Kelm's 1994 essay. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

proposed_edges.relationship: Bohaker: Anishinaabe doodem (kinship) networks, not French alliance alone, carried Great Lakes peoples through the seventeenth-century wars (2006)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stage 2: the essay (WMQ 63:1, 2006, 23–52) is unread. Named readers read: Isaac (2021, para. 4), White's belief that 'shattered' communities 'were only able to rebuild themselves with support from a French alliance—an idea Heidi Bohaker, among others, has disproven'; Fontella (2022, p. 6) lists Bohaker and Rushforth for 'interpretações divergentes sobre a emergência do middle ground'. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§1.2–1.3)

proposed_edges.relationship: P. Deloria asked 'What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?' (2006): the concept's loose use by others, and its relation to the frontier
proposed_edges.map_label: P. Deloria on the middle ground, 2006
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stage 2: the essay (WMQ 63:1, 2006, 15ff.) is unread, and the two readers read give different emphases. Fontella (2022, p. 6) lists 'o pouco rigor na aplicação do conceito (DELORIA, 2006)' and 'a estreita relação do conceito do middle ground com o de fronteira'; Avila (2011, p. 272) reads Deloria as seeing that White did not reduce the middle ground to the frontier. The kind (critique or comparison) cannot be settled without the essay. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§1.1, 1.9)

proposed_edges.relationship: Rushforth: Native slavery and the Fox Wars as the limits of the French–Algonquian alliance (2006)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stage 2: only the title and the essay's opening (OpenAlex) are seen; Fontella (2022, p. 6) lists Rushforth with Bohaker for divergent interpretations of the middle ground's emergence. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.9)

proposed_edges.relationship: Barr: in the Texas borderlands she 'flatly rejects the idea of a “middle ground”' (Gerona on Peace Came in the Form of a Woman, 2007)
proposed_edges.map_label: Barr: no middle ground in Texas, 2007
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stage 2 by coordinator decision: Gerona's H-Atlantic review (December 2008; passages read) says Barr 'flatly rejects the idea of a “middle ground,” at least for Texas'. proposed_edges.relationship: Proposes 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory from the space of “native North American anthropology”' (2007)
proposed_edges.map_label: Simpson: away from the ethnohistorical paradigm, 2007
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, 'On Ethnographic Refusal', Junctures 9 (2007), read in full by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.1): pp. 70–71 (the quotation); p. 71, Iroquois Studies 'quite literally took off where Morgan left off, and as such is a documentary form' and 'seeks to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them'; Morgan's League 'a paradigmatic text of reconstructed and salvage ethnography'. No individual ethnohistorian is named in those pages, so the arrow goes to the field. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_03); drafted here because the edge ends in ethnohistory. Agent B's ihB_rel_02 (audra_simpson → anthropology) carries the anthropology side.

proposed_edges.relationship: Helped the Newberry Library inaugurate its centre for the study of Indian history (1972) and directed its first fellows (1973–74); Iverson judged that the centre, under Jennings and Hoxie, 'has become an extremely influential place' (1993)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Iverson, introduction to the 1993 reissue of Native American Tribalism, p. v, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.9): 'before his death in 1977, McNickle had helped the Newberry Library of Chicago inaugurate the center for the study of Indian history that now bears his name'; first fellows 1973–74 with McNickle as director; under 'Francis Jennings and Frederick Hoxie, [it] has become an extremely influential place'. Hoxie's remark that it 'has had a clear impact on the writing and teaching of Native American history' is as reported by Iverson and is not used as a quotation here. The 1972 founding and the 1984 naming rest on the existing finding-aid record (indexed). Placed in ethnohistory because the centre's programme belongs to the US Native-centred history that the field's roster (Jennings's successors, Calloway, Richter) represents; Agent B requested it (ihB_rel_26).

row.context: Writes the Arkansas Valley as a native ground in which Quapaw and Osage power incorporated colonists; in Piker's and Isaac's quotation, 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground'. Book known through named readers.
Comanche power as an empire that, in Grillot's reading, left 'little or no middle ground for compromise'; White's 2011 preface concurs for this case. Book known through named readers.
row.works: The Comanche Empire (2008); with Samuel Truett, 'On Borderlands' (2011); 'The Shapes of Power' (2014)

row.context: An Anishinaabe-centred Native New World in which, as quoted by Reda, European possession of the interior 'never occurred'. Book known through a named reader.

Writes the Great Basin through colonial violence (2006) and, in 2023, calls 'Indigenous absence' 'a long tradition of American historical analysis'. No text read here connects him to White's middle ground.
row.works: Violence over the Land (2006); The Rediscovery of America (2023)

row.context: Stó:lō identity and historical consciousness across colonialism, written, in Knickerbocker's words, with 'a micro-ethnohistorical lens' and 'extensive use of oral history interviews'. Book known through a named reader; the Stó:lō community–university practice belongs to Community-engaged research.
row.works: The Power of Place, the Problem of Time (2010)

row.context: Proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm' in Iroquois studies (2007). A critic of the field, not a member; no identity classification is recorded on this roster.
Helped the Newberry Library inaugurate its centre for the study of Indian history (1972) and directed its first fellows (1973–74), per Iverson (1993).
row.works: They Came Here First (1949); Native American Tribalism (1973); Newberry centre (1972)

new_sources.citation: Leandro Goya Fontella, 'Entrevista escrita com o Prof. Richard White (Universidade de Stanford) por Leandro Goya Fontella', História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054.

verification.note: Read in full (open access, 27 pp.). The answers were received by email on 30 April 2021 in English; the published text is Fontella's own Portuguese translation ('tradução livre', p. 1 note), so White's answers may only be paraphrased or quoted in Portuguese, never given as English quotations. Pages are the article's own 'N DE 27' folios. Passages: p. 10, the New Indian History 'parece bastante primitiva agora' and the agency argument 'poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 10, 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; p. 15, 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16, upstreaming assumes a belief or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda'; p. 15, a middle ground needs 'um frágil equilíbrio de poder'. Fontella's p. 6 summary of the 2006 WMQ forum is a named reader's account. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)
